title: warp-idle-tail-shadowing-investigation-may-2026
content:
Summary:

This note captures a targeted investigation into a persistent tail in request latency that correlates with long periods of SM idle/wait time after the main compute kernels finish. Working hypothesis: asynchronous copies and small follow-up kernels (housekeeping kernels for KV cache writes, logits postprocessing) create a "shadowing" effect where SM occupancy briefly collapses and then re-populates inefficiently, producing a long tail of low-throughput kernel bursts. This doc documents the Nsight runs, CUDA Graph capture behavior, measured occupancy/timeline patterns, and recommended mitigations to reduce the latency tail and increase sustained GFLOPS across end-to-end requests.

Motivation / symptom:
- Percentile latency spike (p95->p99) for 2048-token generation workloads on H100 served model variants when load is steady.
- Token throughput drops ~18% for tail tokens vs median when burst of requests arrive.
- Trace correlation shows repeated sequences of small kernels interleaved with cudaMemcpyAsync that appear to fragment SM occupancy.

Environment / testbed:
- HW: NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM (single GPU per container)
- CUDA: 12.2
- Driver: 535.XX
- Nsight Systems: 2025.5 (collected with --trace=context,memcpy,cudaProfilerApi)
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit a7d1b2f) with persistent kernel option toggles
- Model: trimmed-llama-13b-fp16 (looped token generation + kv cache)
- Sequence lengths: prompt 256 + gen up to 2048 tokens (avg token length per request variable)
- Microbatching: dynamic microbatch to 4 tokens per microbatch in these experiments
- CUDA Graph capture: capturing capture segments per request window (experimented with per-layer and whole-iteration captures)

Repro steps (short):
1) Start serving runtime locally on H100 VM with perf tracing enabled.
2) Warmup: 50 requests of ~512 tokens.
3) Load generator: steady 12 RPS with 150 concurrency, synthetic prompts.
4) Collect 2-minute Nsight trace and also run nvprof-style occupancy counters via CUPTI sampling.
5) Run with and without CUDA Graph capture enabled; run with persistent kernel on/off.

Key observations from Nsight timelines (representative):
- Sequence pattern: compute-heavy kernel (Transformer attention/FFN) -> small wrapper kernel (kv-downsample/kv-store write, logits squeeze) -> cudaMemcpyAsync(host <-> device for telemetry + pinned buffers) -> small cleanup kernel. This pattern repeats per microbatch.
- During the small kernel + memcpy phase, SM active warps drop from 90% to <8% for ~600-900us per microbatch. The compute kernels resume afterwards but show a ramp-up period where occupancy slowly returns instead of instantly saturating.
- CUDA Graph capture reduced API overhead but made the shadowing worse when capture segments included the small cleanup kernels: graph replay serialized the small kernels and copies in a way that prevented overlapping and merged them into longer sequential windows.
- Persistent kernels (single-stream persistent-thread-block approach) reduced the amplitude of the tail in some test runs but introduced thrashing when KV writes had variable size per microbatch.

Counters and metrics (from CUPTI/occupancy sampling):
- Median SM occupancy during big kernels: 78%-92% (good)
- Occupancy during tail phases: 4%-12% (bad)
- SM active cycles lost across request: ~12% (area under curve) compared to ideal continuous compute stream
- Warp stall reasons in NVTX annotated trace: long memory dependency stalls (cache miss + pending async copy), then scheduler starvation during tiny kernel launches

Hypothesis details:
1) Small kernels act as scheduling fences on the GPU and, combined with host-side pinned buffer transfers, break the continuous stream of work that keeps SMs warm.
2) CUDA Graph capture that implicitly serializes operations expands these fences into longer contiguous periods of low occupancy.
3) Persistent kernel model helps by keeping threads resident and reducing launch overhead, but is sensitive to variability in the amount of KV write work (can force intra-SM load imbalance).

Experiment matrix and outcomes (high level):
- Baseline (no graphs, no persistent kernels): p95 latency X, p99 latency Y, tail occupancy loss 12%
- With CUDA Graph capture (per-request): p95 slightly improved, p99 worsened (+6-9%); tail occupancy loss increased to ~18%
- With CUDA Graph capture but grouping only compute kernels (exclude memcpy/housekeeping): p99 improved by ~4% vs baseline; tail loss down to ~9%
- Persistent kernel ON (no graphs): p99 improved sometimes (-5%), unstable for variable KV sizes
- Persistent kernel + selective graph capture (compute-only replay): best median and tail in lab (p99 -7%).

Experiment logs (snippets):
- Trace snippet (annotated timeline entries, durations approximate):
  00:00:00.000 compute_attention_kernel grid=(1024,1,1) t=3.2ms occupancy~85%
  00:00:00.003 kv_store_write kernel grid=(32,1,1) t=0.85ms occupancy~6%
  00:00:00.004 cudaMemcpyAsync(pinned->device) t=1.1ms (stream 2)
  00:00:00.005 cleanup_kernel grid=(16,1,1) t=0.5ms occupancy~4%
  00:00:00.0058 compute_ffn_kernel grid=(1024,1,1) t=2.8ms occupancy ramping 20%->70%

Interpretation and root causes (concise):
- Frequent tiny kernels and interleaved async copies create fragmentation: each tiny kernel doesn't use enough warps to keep many SMs busy, then the memcpy introduces a scheduling gap and cache/MEM warmup costs for the next big kernel.
- Graph capture that captures everything increases serialization and removes chance for host-driven overlap that can otherwise hide some memcpy latency.
- Persistent kernel approach reduces launch overhead but needs careful partitioning of persistent threads vs housekeeping work.

Immediate mitigation recommendations (practical):
1) Selective CUDA Graph capture: capture only compute-heavy kernels (attention/FFN/MatMuls). Exclude small KV housekeeping kernels and telemetry memcpy operations from the graph. This preserves replay efficiency and allows host-driven overlap for cleanup copies.
2) Fuse tiny housekeeping kernels into a single coalesced kernel that performs KV write + small postprocessing in one launch. Aim for launch occupancy >= 32 warps.
3) Batch memcpy operations: aggregate small pinned-buffer copies into larger batched transfers or move telemetry off the hot-path into a separate streaming pipeline (dedicated stream with lower priority).
4) Introduce stream priorities and assign housekeeping/copy streams lower priority so compute work can preempt when needed (validate on H100; verify with preemption counters).
5) Experimentally gate persistent kernel mode: enable persistent kernels only when KV write size variance < threshold to avoid thrashing. Add auto-telemetry to measure KV variance and flip modes dynamically.
6) Add a thin backoff: if occupancy ramp is slow, inject a light-weight prefetch (touch memory) before launching big kernels to warm caches (cheap host-to-device pinned touch or a small read kernel).

Longer-term / research actions:
- Kernel fusion exploration: create prototypes that combine KV-store writes and logits postprocessing inside the same compute kernel, measure occupancy and cache behavior.
- CUDA Graph replay tuning: test segmented graph replays where compute segments are replayed frequently and housekeeping segments are replayed asynchronously to maintain overlap.
- Scheduler-level experiments with occupancy-aware launch parameters: tune block sizes and __launch_bounds__ for the most common sequence lengths to increase sustained occupancy.
- Evaluate NVLink peer-to-peer effects when multi-GPU (we saw slightly different tail characteristics when cross-GPU copies exist).

Quick checklist to reduce tail in next sprint (owner assigned):
- [ ] PR: exclude housekeeping kernels from capture (Marcus Li) -> github PR #748 (linked)
- [ ] Prototype: fused-kv-write kernel (Diego Ramos) -> branch fused-kv-write
- [ ] Perf test: selective graph + stream priorities run across 3 H100 nodes (Ellen Park) -> bench suite run id: perfrun-2026-05-18
- [ ] Instrumentation: measure KV_size variance and expose metric to autoscaler (Priya Menon)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is the occupancy ramp influenced more by L2 cache coldness from memcpy or by SM scheduling starvation due to tiny kernel size? Need microbench to isolate memory warmup vs scheduling gaps.
- Does enabling cooperative groups for small kernels provide better SM fill than simple launches?
- Tradeoffs in power/thermal when persistent kernel runs continuously on H100 for prolonged periods.

Appendix: quick commands used
- Nsight capture: nsys profile --output=run-2026-05-14 --trace=nvtx,osrt,cudaMemcpy,nvtx --sample=none ./serving-runtime --trace-nsight
- Simple occupancy probe (CUPTI sample script): python tools/occupancy_probe.py --interval-ms 10 --duration-s 120 --gpu 0
- CUDA Graph capture pattern: graphBegin(); for (each compute kernel) graphAddLaunch(...); graphEnd();

Notes / conversational fragments (raw):
- "I feel like the memcpy pattern is the worst offender when microbatching to small token windows"
- "Maybe we accidentally optimized for median latency at the cost of tail because fused graphs hide overlap heuristics"
- "Persistent kernel could be a win if we can make the KV writes deterministic or bounded"

If you want, I can extract a short checklist PR description and performance regression tests to attach to PR #748. Also happy to run an automated microbench to prove whether memory warmup or scheduler starvation dominates.

End of note.
